title: Looker vs Power BI: Retail Analytics APAC Comparison
summary: A Looker vs Power BI retail analytics APAC comparison across semantic layers, BigQuery and Shopify connectors, multi-currency reporting, cost and embedding.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Power BI wins on cost and speed for Microsoft 365 organisations with under 30 builders and internal-only reporting. Looker wins where BigQuery is the warehouse, multiple entities and currencies need one enforced metric definition, or dashboards must be embedded for external merchants, franchisees or dealers.


---


Most Looker vs Power BI retail analytics APAC comparison posts argue about chart types. That is the least important variable. In almost every retail analytics project I have seen across Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and Australia, the bottleneck was never visualisation — it was that three systems disagreed on what "net sales" meant, and nobody could tell you which FX rate a HKD-reporting P&L used for a TWD marketplace order refunded 40 days later.

Pick the wrong tool and you lose some money. Pick the wrong semantic model and you lose the trust of your commercial team, which costs far more. So this comparison is organised around the six things that actually break in APAC retail: semantic layer governance, connectors to Shopify and BigQuery, multi-currency and multi-entity reporting, licence cost at scale, embedded analytics for marketplace and franchise dashboards, and the local skills market.


*Related reading:*[Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus Migration Playbook: 9 Phased Steps](https://branch8.com/posts/adobe-commerce-to-shopify-plus-migration-playbook)


## The verdict, before you scroll


**Choose Power BI** if your organisation already runs Microsoft 365 E3/E5, your analytics team is under roughly 30 people, your data lives in a mix of SQL Server, Dynamics, Excel exports and a Shopify or marketplace feed, and your reporting consumers are internal staff. The economics are hard to beat, and Microsoft's Fabric roadmap means the platform is not going anywhere.


**Choose Looker** (the Google Cloud enterprise product, not Looker Studio) if you have a BigQuery warehouse, more than one country or entity, multiple teams that will all claim their own version of gross margin, and a requirement to embed dashboards into a merchant portal, franchise extranet or dealer system. LookML's version-controlled modelling layer is the single strongest argument for Looker, and it is a governance argument, not a visualisation one.


**Choose neither yet** if you cannot currently answer, in one query, what a single order looked like after discounts, returns, marketplace commission and FX conversion. Buy the warehouse and the modelling work first. A BI licence on top of unreconciled data just industrialises the argument.


## Clearing up the Looker vs Looker Studio confusion first


Half the Reddit threads comparing these tools are comparing the wrong products. Google sells two things with similar names, per the[Google Cloud Looker documentation](https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs) :


- **Looker** — the enterprise platform with LookML, a Git-backed semantic modelling language, row-level permissions, an API and embedded analytics SDK. Priced by platform plus per-user licensing, quoted rather than listed.
- **Looker Studio** — the free, formerly-Data-Studio dashboarding tool, with a paid **Looker Studio Pro** tier for team management and SLA support.


When people on r/analytics say "Looker Studio is fine and free," they are right for a single-brand DTC store pulling Google Ads and GA4. When people say "Looker's modelling layer changed how our company works," they mean the enterprise product. Comparing Looker Studio to Power BI Pro is comparing a free visualiser to a modelling engine. Comparing Looker to Power BI Premium is a real decision.


For the rest of this article, "Looker" means the enterprise platform unless stated.

## Dimension 1: Semantic layer flexibility


This is where the two platforms genuinely diverge in philosophy.


**Looker / LookML.** You define dimensions, measures and joins once in` .lkml` files that live in Git. Every dashboard, Explore and API call resolves against that definition. A margin change is a pull request.


```text
1  view: orders {    2    sql_table_name: `analytics.fct_orders` ;;    3
4    dimension_group: created {    5      type: time    6      timeframes: [date, week, month, fiscal_quarter]    7      sql: ${TABLE}.created_at ;;    8    }    9
10    measure: net_sales_hkd {    11      type: sum    12      sql: ${TABLE}.gross_sales_local    13           * ${TABLE}.fx_rate_to_hkd    14           - ${TABLE}.discount_local * ${TABLE}.fx_rate_to_hkd ;;    15      value_format_name: hkd    16    }    17  }
```


The practical effect in a multi-market retailer: when Finance redefines net sales to exclude shipping revenue, one merge request updates every dashboard in Hong Kong, Taipei and Sydney simultaneously. No one is left on a stale local copy.


**Power BI / semantic models.** Power BI has had a semantic layer for years — it was called a dataset, and Microsoft renamed it to "semantic model," as covered in the[Power BI documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/power-bi/) . Measures are written in DAX, and shared semantic models can be certified and reused by report authors.


```text
1  Net Sales (HKD) =    2  SUMX(    3      'fct_orders',    4      ( 'fct_orders'[gross_sales_local] - 'fct_orders'[discount_local] )    5        * RELATED( 'dim_fx'[rate_to_hkd] )    6  )
```


The capability is real. The governance is weaker by default. Anyone with Power BI Desktop can download a model, fork it, add their own measure and publish a near-identical workspace. Microsoft's answer is endorsement and certification workflows plus deployment pipelines — good features, but opt-in discipline rather than enforced structure.


**Honest trade-off:** LookML forces rigour and therefore forces a slower, engineer-dependent change cycle. If your merchandising lead wants a new metric by Thursday, Power BI gets there faster; Looker gets there correctly. Pick based on which failure mode hurts you more.


## Dimension 2: Shopify, BigQuery and marketplace connectors


APAC retail stacks are rarely clean. A typical mid-market group I see runs Shopify Plus for DTC, Shopee or Lazada for Southeast Asia, Tmall Global or a WeChat Mini Program for China, a POS system for physical stores, and SAP or Oracle NetSuite for finance.


**Looker's position** is strongest when BigQuery is the warehouse. Looker generates SQL and pushes it down to the warehouse — there is no separate extract to refresh, so a mega-sale dashboard reflects whatever landed in BigQuery seconds ago. Google's own[BigQuery documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs) details streaming inserts that make this practical during 11.11 or 6.18 peaks. Shopify's Bulk Operations API and the connectors in the[Shopify developer documentation](https://shopify.dev/docs) land raw order data; dbt or Dataform models it; LookML exposes it.


**Power BI's position** is strongest when the warehouse is Azure Synapse, Fabric OneLake, or SQL Server. DirectQuery exists and works against BigQuery too, but the default and best-trodden path is Import mode into a VertiPaq in-memory model. That gives excellent dashboard response times and a refresh-schedule dependency. Power BI Pro caps scheduled refreshes at eight per day; Premium capacity raises that to 48, per Microsoft's published[Power BI pricing](https://powerbi.microsoft.com/pricing/) and capacity documentation.


For a flash-sale war room where merchandisers are repricing hourly, 48 refreshes is every 30 minutes. That may be fine. It is not real-time, and teams that assume it is get burned on the day it matters most.


**Where both are equal:** neither has credible native connectors for Shopee, Lazada, Tmall or Rakuten. You will build or buy that ingestion regardless — Fivetran, Airbyte, or a custom extractor hitting the open platform APIs. Do not let a vendor demo convince you otherwise.

## Dimension 3: Multi-currency and multi-entity reporting


This is the most underrated dimension in any APAC BI evaluation, and it is mostly a modelling problem rather than a tool problem.


A regional retailer selling in HKD, SGD, TWD, MYR, IDR and AUD needs at minimum:


- **Transaction currency** — what the customer actually paid.
- **Functional currency** — the operating entity's books.
- **Group reporting currency** — the consolidated view.
- **A rate policy** — transaction-date rate, month-average rate, or closing rate, and which one applies to a return booked in a later period.


IDR amounts in the hundreds of millions alongside HKD amounts in the hundreds also break naive number formatting on the same chart.


**Looker** handles this well because the conversion logic sits in LookML with user attributes controlling which currency a viewer sees. One Explore, six currency views, one definition of the rate policy.


**Power BI** handles it through DAX measures and role-based security, which also works, but the logic tends to be duplicated across reports unless you are strict about a single certified semantic model. I have seen three Power BI workspaces in one group each applying a different FX rate source — none of them wrong individually, all of them irreconcilable in a board pack.


The real recommendation: put FX conversion in the warehouse as a materialised column on the fact table, with a dated rate dimension, before it reaches either BI tool. Then both platforms behave. The tool is downstream of the problem.


## Dimension 4: Licence cost at realistic APAC scale


Public list pricing tells part of the story. Microsoft lists Power BI Pro and Power BI Premium Per User on its[pricing page](https://powerbi.microsoft.com/pricing/) , with Pro included in Microsoft 365 E5 — which is why so many enterprises find Power BI effectively pre-paid. Google does not publish Looker list pricing; it is quoted per deployment, combining a platform fee with Developer, Standard and Viewer user tiers.


The cost comparison that matters is not per-seat. It is:


### Total cost components to model


- **Licences** — seats plus capacity or platform fee.
- **Warehouse compute** — Looker's push-down architecture means every dashboard interaction is a BigQuery query. BigQuery's on-demand pricing bills by bytes scanned, per[Google's pricing documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing) . Unpartitioned tables plus curious executives equals a surprising bill. Partitioning, clustering and Looker's aggregate awareness are mitigations, not optional extras.
- **Implementation labour** — LookML development is a specialist skill. DAX is also specialist, but the pool of people who know it in Hong Kong, Manila and Kuala Lumpur is substantially larger.
- **Ongoing modelling maintenance** — the recurring cost nobody budgets.


A common pattern: Power BI's licence line is lower and its labour line is lower, while Looker's licence line is higher but its rework line is lower because the model is enforced. For a 15-person analytics function on Microsoft 365, Power BI almost always wins on total cost. Past roughly 100 report consumers across several entities, the gap narrows and governance savings start to matter.


I will not invent a break-even number for your situation. Build the four-line model above with your actual seat counts and your actual query volume before signing anything.

## Dimension 5: Embedded analytics for marketplace and partner dashboards


If you run a marketplace, a franchise network or a dealer channel, you need to show third parties their own numbers and nobody else's. This is where the two products separate sharply.


**Looker** was built for this. The embed SDK, signed embed URLs and user attributes map cleanly onto a multi-tenant permission model. You set a user attribute for` merchant_id` , apply it as an access filter in LookML, and every query is scoped automatically — the filter lives in the model, not in the application that calls it.


```text
1  access_filter: {    2    field: orders.merchant_id    3    user_attribute: merchant_id    4  }
```


**Power BI Embedded** also does multi-tenancy, through the app-owns-data pattern with row-level security roles passed in the embed token. It works. The Azure capacity SKUs (A/F series) are a separate billing line from your internal Power BI estate, and the implementation involves more application-side code to generate and scope tokens. Microsoft documents the pattern thoroughly in the[Power BI embedded analytics documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/power-bi/developer/embedded/) .


In Branch8 engagements with manufacturers selling through dealer networks, the deciding factor has consistently been where the tenancy logic should live. Teams that want permissions enforced centrally in the data model lean Looker. Teams that already have a mature application with its own auth layer and want BI as a rendered component lean Power BI Embedded.


## Dimension 6: The APAC skills and support reality


Tool evaluations run in Singapore or Hong Kong often ignore hiring.


Power BI skills are abundant across the region. Microsoft certification pathways are well established, and you can staff a Power BI team in Manila, Ho Chi Minh City or Kuala Lumpur without a long search. Local Microsoft partner coverage is dense in every APAC market.


Looker and LookML skills are scarcer and concentrated in Singapore, Sydney and a handful of Hong Kong teams. Google Cloud's regional presence is strong — the asia-east2 (Hong Kong), asia-southeast1 (Singapore) and australia-southeast1 (Sydney) regions matter for data residency under Singapore's PDPA or Australia's Privacy Act — but the consultant pool is thinner. Factor a longer hiring cycle, or a managed partner arrangement, into the plan.


There is also a practical language dimension. If your Taipei merchandising team works primarily in Traditional Chinese and your Jakarta team in Bahasa Indonesia, check localisation support for both the interface and your own field labels during the trial, not after.

## When to choose Power BI


- You already hold Microsoft 365 E5, making Power BI Pro a sunk cost.
- Your analytics team is small — roughly under 30 active builders — and needs to move fast without a dedicated modelling engineer.
- Your source systems skew Microsoft: Dynamics 365, SQL Server, SharePoint, Excel-heavy finance processes.
- Reporting consumers are internal: store managers, buyers, regional heads.
- You need strong Excel interoperability, because your CFO will export to Excel no matter what you build.
- Hourly or half-hourly data freshness is sufficient for your peak-trading decisions.


## When to choose Looker


- BigQuery is already your warehouse, or you are committing to Google Cloud.
- You operate across multiple countries, entities and currencies and need one enforced definition of every metric.
- You need true real-time query behaviour during mega-sale events rather than scheduled refreshes.
- You are embedding dashboards for external parties — merchants, franchisees, dealers, suppliers — with strict tenant isolation.
- Your data team already works in Git, dbt and code review, so LookML fits existing practice.
- Metric disputes between Finance and Commercial are a recurring, expensive problem.

## Where Tableau fits, briefly


People searching Looker vs Power BI vs Tableau usually want to know if they are missing something. Tableau remains the strongest pure visual-analysis tool for analysts exploring data interactively, and Salesforce integration is an advantage if your CRM is Salesforce Commerce Cloud. Its semantic layer sits between the other two: more structured than ad-hoc Power BI, less enforced than LookML. Gartner's Peer Insights listings for[analytics and BI platforms](https://www.gartner.com/reviews/market/analytics-business-intelligence-platforms) show all three clustered tightly on user ratings, which tells you the differentiation is contextual rather than absolute. If Tableau is not already in your stack, it rarely wins a greenfield APAC retail evaluation on cost.


## A decision framework you can run in a week


Score each question yes or no. Count the leans.


### 1. Warehouse gravity


Is your warehouse BigQuery? → Looker. Synapse, Fabric or SQL Server? → Power BI. Snowflake or Databricks? → genuinely neutral; move to question 2.


### 2. Licence pre-payment


Do you hold Microsoft 365 E5 across the organisation? → strong Power BI lean on cost alone.


### 3. Audience boundary


Will external parties view dashboards? → Looker lean. Internal only? → Power BI lean.


### 4. Metric dispute frequency


Have two departments presented different numbers for the same KPI in the last quarter? → Looker lean. Never happens? → Power BI lean.


### 5. Freshness requirement


Do peak-trading decisions need sub-15-minute data? → Looker lean. Hourly is fine? → Power BI lean.


### 6. Team composition


Do you have, or can you hire, an engineer who will own the semantic model as code? → Looker is viable. If not, Looker will become shelfware with a large invoice attached.


Four or more leans in one direction is a decision. A split means your data foundation is the actual project, not your BI tool.

## What to do Monday morning


**1. Run the single-order reconciliation test.** Pick one order from last month that was discounted, partially returned and placed through a marketplace in a non-home currency. Trace it end-to-end through your current reporting. If you cannot do it in under an hour, your problem is upstream of any Looker vs Power BI retail analytics APAC comparison, and no licence fixes it.


**2. Pull your actual seat and query numbers.** Count distinct report consumers by entity, count builders, and if you are on BigQuery, pull last month's bytes-scanned total. These three figures drive the entire cost model. Build the four-line total-cost sheet before you take a vendor call.


**3. Book both trials with the same brief.** Give each vendor or partner the same three dashboards to build — a multi-currency group P&L, a marketplace merchant view with tenant isolation, and a live peak-trading sales monitor. Judge on how the semantic model looks after week two, not on how the demo looks on day one.
